title: Cutter v. Powell
lead: Thomas Cutter died after serving as second mate for most of a voyage to Liverpool. His estate sought payment for that service, but the ship’s master had promised an unusually large lump sum only if Cutter served through the voyage.

actors.name: Thomas Cutter
actors.role: Second mate aboard the Governor Parry

actors.name: Powell
actors.role: Defendant and master of the ship

actors.name: Cutter’s administratrix
actors.role: Representative of Cutter’s estate seeking compensation

actors.name: Lord Kenyon, Ashhurst, Grose, and Lawrence
actors.role: The four King’s Bench judges who explained the result

proceedings: A Lancaster jury returned a plaintiff’s verdict for £31 10s., subject to the King’s Bench’s opinion on stated facts. On June 9, 1795, the King’s Bench directed a postea for the defendant unless further evidence of usage was supplied before term ended; no further mention is reported.
limits: This is a historical construction of this particular compensation bargain, not a statement of modern maritime wage law. The judges left room for an established contrary trade usage. Later editorial discussions in the reprint are not holdings of Cutter.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A larger payment depends on completing the voyage
paragraphs: At Kingston, Jamaica, on July 31, 1793, Powell, master of the Governor Parry, gave Thomas Cutter a written promise of thirty guineas. Payment would come ten days after arrival at Liverpool, provided Cutter proceeded, continued, and performed his duty as second mate throughout the passage. Cutter boarded that day. The ship sailed on August 2, and he performed his duty until he died on September 20. The ship reached Liverpool on October 9. Nothing in the stated facts attributed his failure to finish to desertion, misconduct, or fault.

A second mate hired by the month for an outward-and-home voyage ordinarily earned £4 per month. Seamen hired for the run from Jamaica to England commonly received a gross sum, and that voyage usually lasted about eight weeks. Thirty guineas equaled £31 10s., nearly four times the roughly £8 that two months at the ordinary monthly rate would yield. That difference would become central to the judges' understanding of the bargain; it was not a damages calculation for Cutter's actual service.

sources.pinpoint: Stated facts and compensation comparison, Smith reprint 1212–1213, 1215, 1217

sections.title: The estate asks for the value of the work
paragraphs: Cutter's administratrix, acting for his estate, sued Powell in assumpsit for the work and labor Cutter had performed. Powell pleaded the general issue. A Lancaster jury found for the administratrix for £31 10s., but made its verdict subject to the King's Bench's legal decision on the stated case.

J. Haywood argued for the estate in the preceding term. The court postponed decision to investigate commercial usage. When argument resumed, Chambre represented the administratrix and Wood represented Powell. Examples from merchants showed some paying all wages after a death and others paying a proportion. Those examples did not establish a settled practice.

The estate sought proportionate compensation on a quantum meruit, a claim for the value of the service. The ship had completed its voyage and earned freight, so a rule tying wages to freight did not defeat payment. Cutter's blameless death also differed from desertion. Wiggins v. Ingleton, involving a seaman impressed into public service, and Edwards v. Child, allowing compensation for an outward passage despite capture on the return, supplied examples of payment after interrupted service.

The administratrix characterized the note as security for the promised sum, with a condition encouraging good conduct, rather than a complete exclusion of all other compensation. Alternatively, even if failure to complete barred the thirty guineas, she argued that the express promise addressed only completed service; an implied undertaking could still pay for work actually supplied.

sources.pinpoint: Procedure and plaintiff’s arguments, 1212–1215 and authority notes

sections.title: The master insists on the agreed condition
sections.cue: An express bargain against an implied obligation
paragraphs: Powell answered that the agreement was entire and indivisible. Cutter had chosen a chance to earn much more than monthly wages in exchange for serving throughout the passage. His estate could not substitute a different implied arrangement when the express condition failed. Ordinary yearly hiring, in which an executor might recover a proportion after the worker's death, was different from this unusually large and expressly conditional payment. Neither earned freight nor an innocent death fulfilled the condition.

Wood illustrated his argument with contractual losses borne despite innocence, including maritime loss and rent following a house fire. Chief Justice Lord Kenyon qualified the rent illustration by referring to equitable relief where a tenant surrendered the lease. That exchange did not resolve a separate landlord-tenant dispute; later editorial authorities about it were not part of the court's holding here.

sections.title: Kenyon and Ashhurst enforce this particular allocation
paragraphs: Kenyon confined his decision to the stated facts and this agreement, declining to settle all marine contracts. Where parties expressly fixed compensation, the law would not imply an inconsistent obligation. The unusually high payment supported an all-or-nothing arrangement. His comparison to insurance described the allocation of compensation risk: Cutter would receive the larger amount for completing the duty, but nothing under this bargain if he did not. It did not mean that Cutter bought a separate insurance policy.

Kenyon remained open to evidence of usage. The recently reported Liverpool examples were insufficient, but a universal commercial understanding giving such notes a different meaning would cause him to abandon his construction.

Justice Ashhurst likewise treated complete performance as a condition precedent to payment. The estate could not discard the express agreement merely because an implied one would be more favorable. Cutter was blameless, but lack of blame neither satisfied the condition nor created a right contrary to the agreement.

sections.title: Grose and Lawrence keep commercial usage in view
paragraphs: Justice Grose had examined the laws of Oleron and merchant practice. He also considered Chandler v. Greaves, where a sailor put ashore with a broken leg recovered full wages and a new trial was refused. Grose did not know the precise grounds of that decision, and his own inquiries were not satisfactory enough to establish a governing usage. This agreement's large conditional payment therefore supported thirty guineas for complete service or nothing under the promise. He suggested further investigation of how these commonly used notes had been construed.

Justice Lawrence compared an entire-service agreement reported in Salkeld: a promise of £100 for a year did not support a £75 claim for three quarters. Ordinary hired service could be understood differently, permitting proportionate payment, and proven usage could similarly support Cutter's estate. In its absence, this express entire bargain controlled. Lawrence also suggested that impressed-seaman cases might be exceptional because the king's officers commonly supplied a replacement, preserving service for the owner; he did not announce a universal rule for interruptions by public authority.

On June 9, 1795, all four judges favored Powell on the evidence before them. The report directed the postea to the defendant unless additional information about usage was supplied before the term ended. The case was not mentioned again. The estate consequently recovered neither the thirty guineas nor proportionate compensation in this proceeding. The result concerned entitlement to payment under the bargain, even though death involved no wrongdoing.
